strengths: Addresses an important and timely real-world safety problem with concrete motivating evidence from in-the-wild experiments
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 15 LLMs and 3 agent scaffolds with rigorous methodology and extensive ablations
Well-designed three-stage test case generation framework with automated quality filtering and clear attainability/integrity criteria
Simulation-based testing carefully engineered to avoid real-world harms while maintaining experimental fidelity
High inter-annotator agreement for safety evaluation (95-98%) validates the checklist-assisted evaluation approach
Honest and thorough discussion of limitations, including simulation-to-real gap analysis in Section E.5
Valuable benchmark contribution (300 test cases across 5 risk types) with promised code release will benefit the community
Clear presentation with well-structured content, effective visualizations, and comprehensive supplementary details
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty—framework combines existing techniques (LLM-assisted generation, simulation-based testing, LLM-as-a-Judge) without significant innovation in individual components
Dramatic variation in test case retention rates (6.8-31.3%) raises concerns about quality uniformity; unclear whether low retention indicates generation failures or overly strict filtering criteria
Shallow mechanistic analysis—while high-level findings are documented, the paper lacks deep investigation into why agents fail (e.g., only GPT-5-mini analyzed in detail in Section D)
Weak mitigation strategies—only two simple defenses tested; filtering achieves only 44.2% recall; knowledge-action gap identified but unexplored; no proposed solutions

Simulation-based testing limitations underexplored—only one unreliable website per query, no testing of coordinated multi-source attacks, position bias shown significant (Figure 8) but default choice may understate real risks
Evaluator design concerns—using GPT-4.1-mini to evaluate other GPT models introduces potential circularity; LLM-based helpfulness evaluation may conflate plausibility with actual helpfulness
Website generation fidelity unvalidated—claim of 'highly plausible' websites lacks human validation; similar performance across generators (Figure 9) suggests websites may lack sophistication

Findings are largely confirmatory rather than surprising—that GPT-5 is safer, deep research enables robustness, and reasoning helps safety align with prior expectations rather than revealing novel insights
Benchmark scale modest (300 cases, 5 risk types, Google Search only) limits comprehensiveness compared to contemporaneous benchmarks
Missing implementation details for reproducibility—persona selection process, health question dataset construction, and total experimental cost not discussed

strengths: Well-motivated problem with supporting in-the-wild experiments demonstrating unreliable search results and their effects on agent behavior
Systematic and well-structured three-stage test generation workflow with thoughtful auxiliary information collection
Comprehensive evaluation across 15 models, 3 agent scaffolds, and 300 test cases with extensive ablation studies
Ethical approach using simulation-based testing to avoid real-world harm with honest discussion of limitations
High inter-rater agreement (96%) on safety evaluation with checklist-assisted approach
Good reproducibility with promised code/test release and detailed configurations in appendices
weaknesses: Limited novelty: combines standard techniques (LLM generation, differential testing, LLM-as-Judge) without conceptual advances or new algorithmic insights
Fundamental validity gap: synthetically generated websites may not reflect realistic threats; unclear how LLM-generated adversarial content compares to actual malicious sites in the wild
Weak in-the-wild evidence: only 4.6% of health queries show behavioral shifts, and 4.3% content farm detection relies on GPT judgment not ground truth—insufficient to establish threat severity
Test case quality concerns: very low retention rates for adversarial risks (6.8-6.9%) raise questions about whether final test set represents realistic threats
Weak defense mechanisms tested: reminder prompting is known ineffective (strawman); filtering achieves only ~50% ASR reduction with 44% recall, offering no practical solutions
Limited actionability: findings are expected (reasoning models safer, deep research helps, misinformation hard); no constructive mitigation strategies proposed
Scope limitations: only Google Search evaluated; proprietary search agents excluded; generalization unclear across services and deployment contexts
LLM-as-Judge evaluation: while 96% agreement on 200 author-annotated examples is reported, generalization to all risk types unvalidated; no comparison to human expert evaluation
Incomplete analysis of GPT-5 safety: case study (Section D) is speculative, relying on shallow interpretation of reasoning summaries without conclusive mechanistic explanation
Statistical rigor: no confidence intervals; only 3 runs per test case; unclear if performance differences are significant

strengths: Important and timely problem: Identifies genuine safety vulnerability in increasingly deployed search agents with compelling motivating experiments showing 4.3% content farms in search results and measurable agent behavior shifts

Rigorous validation methodology: Extensive ablations (injection position, token limits, website generator, timestamps), 95-98% human-LLM agreement on 200 samples, dual-criteria quality filtering, and temporal persistence tests
Comprehensive evaluation: 15 LLMs (7 proprietary, 8 open-source), 3 representative scaffolds, 300 test cases across 5 risk types, with clear findings on vulnerability rates (up to 90.5% ASR)
Practical contributions: Fully automated, scalable framework enabling developers to assess search agent safety; benchmark and code promised for release; reveals knowledge-action gap in LLM safety
Well-designed three-step test generation pipeline: Scenario envisioning, test design with temporal reasoning, and instantiation with guideline-assisted website synthesis and checklist evaluation
Thorough limitation discussion: Thoughtful treatment of simulation-reality gap (Section E.5), generalization boundaries (Google Search only, some systems inaccessible), and benchmark scale
Strong presentation: Clear structure, comprehensive appendices with all prompts and configurations, effective visualizations, and careful ethics consideration with harm mitigation strategies
weaknesses: Fundamental simulation-reality gap: Synthetic website credibility validated only indirectly (44.2% filter recall); injecting at end of results may underestimate attacks achieving top rankings; threat model of single benign query with ≤1 unreliable website is conservative

Limited defense evaluation: Only two simple defenses tested (reminder prompting, basic filtering); no exploration of sophisticated mitigations like uncertainty quantification or source verification; paper identifies problems but offers limited solutions
Test case quality concerns: Very low retention rates for adversarial risks (6.8-6.9%); paper doesn't deeply analyze generation bias or threshold setting; manual review process underspecified

Generalization limitations: Evaluates only Google Search (unclear if findings transfer to Bing, DuckDuckGo); proprietary deep-research systems inaccessible; only 300 cases total (may underrepresent some risk types)

Evaluator validation limited: Only 200 samples validated (~4.4% of test cases); LLM judges can exhibit biases; checklist approach may miss nuanced unsafe behaviors; helpfulness scoring lacks inter-annotator agreement

Incomplete analysis of key phenomena: Why do reasoning models perform better (Section D explanatory, not definitive)? Why does tool-calling outperform workflow (Table 2 interesting but undiscussed)? Why is misinformation most vulnerable (78.3% avg ASR)?
Presentation gaps: Terminology 'ASR' used for non-adversarial risks could be clearer; test case examples in appendix not main text; deep research scaffold details sparse in main paper

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem with real-world evidence of practical relevance (ChatGPT Search leak, 4.3% content farms in search results)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 17 LLMs, 3 scaffolds, 5 risk types with thorough ablation studies validating all major design choices
Thoughtfully designed three-stage test case generation workflow that systematically grounds tests in realistic threat scenarios
Clear, actionable findings about model vulnerabilities and defense ineffectiveness, including discovery of knowledge-action gap in LLM safety
Rigorous supplementary materials with extensive validation (95%+ human-evaluator agreement, detailed ablations across 7 testing configurations)
Ethically sound simulation-based approach with well-justified avoidance of real-world SEO manipulation harms
Reproducibility-focused with commitment to open-source code, dataset, and all prompts used
weaknesses: Significant simulation-to-reality gap: injecting one unreliable website at end of results is conservative; real adversarial attacks may be more sophisticated or coordinated

Test case feasibility concerns: extremely low retention rates for adversarial risks (6.8-6.9% for prompt injection/harmful output) raise questions about whether automated filtering systematically excludes harder scenarios
Circular dependency in evaluation: GPT-4.1-mini used for both test generation and safety evaluation creates potential bias; human validation only by authors, not independent reviewers
Limited failure analysis: main finding of 'uncritical trust' is somewhat obvious; no systematic categorization of failure modes or investigation of which content types fool which models
Website synthesis may lack sophistication of real attacks: generated websites use standard persuasion guidelines; topical relevance requirement may exclude subtle SEO techniques
Shallow defense exploration: only two simple defenses tested; filtering achieves only 44.2% recall with no exploration of better approaches or training-based mitigations
Statistical rigor gaps: no confidence intervals, significance testing, or quantified intra-trial variation; results averaged across only 3 trials
Modest benchmark scale: 300 test cases with uneven distribution across risk types may limit generalizability; no cross-domain analysis

strengths: Well-motivated and timely problem addressing real safety concerns in LLM-based search agents with compelling motivating examples
Comprehensive empirical evaluation covering 17 LLMs, 3 agent scaffolds, and 300 test cases with extensive validation (95%+ human agreement with automated evaluator)
Responsible methodology using simulation-based approach to avoid harmful real-world SEO attacks; thoughtful threat model design with differential testing for quality filtering
Thorough documentation including detailed appendices, prompts, and ablation studies on multiple configuration choices (injection position, token limits, website generation strategies)
Nuanced insights including lack of inherent tension between safety and helpfulness, revelation of knowledge-action gap in LLMs, and analysis of why reasoning models are more resilient
weaknesses: Core methodological limitation: Simulation-based threat model is not validated against real attacks; artificially appended unreliable websites differ fundamentally from algorithmically-ranked malicious content. Suspiciously high ASRs (90.5%) likely reflect artifact of artificial injection point rather than realistic vulnerabilities

Low test case retention rates (6.8%-18.9%) indicate widespread infeasibility of generated test cases; framework generated ~1,300 raw cases to yield 300 usable ones, suggesting fundamental issues with automated test case generation quality and feasibility assessment

LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation concerns: using GPT-4.1-mini as evaluator introduces self-referential bias; only 200 manually validated samples insufficient for 5,100+ test executions; checklist-based evaluation may miss subtle failures not captured in predetermined items

Extremely limited defense evaluation: only two basic defenses tested (reminder prompting and filtering with 44.2% recall); no sophisticated mechanisms, architectural solutions, or actionable guidance for developers on what actually works

Insufficient generalization analysis: single search service (Google), cannot test proprietary systems, English-only, limited architectural diversity; unclear how findings transfer to other search services, languages, or LLM agent designs

Incremental novelty: combines standard LLM prompting, established red-teaming, and checklist evaluation without methodological innovation; main contribution is systematic application at scale rather than novel techniques

Reproducibility limitations: code/data not provided despite open-source claims; heavily dependent on proprietary APIs; expensive to reproduce (costs undisclosed); likely prohibitive for many researchers even if code released

Statistical rigor issues: averaged over only 3 runs per configuration, no confidence intervals or significance testing, no multiple-comparison correction; low website generation sophistication (non-persuasive by default, marginal improvement with explicit requests) raises questions about realism

strengths: Rigorous methodology with well-defined threat model and three-stage test generation pipeline with automated quality filtering
Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 300 test cases × 17 models × 3 scaffolds, covering multiple risk types and agent architectures
Well-grounded problem motivation with concrete in-the-wild observations showing 4.3% content farms in search results and behavioral shifts in 46/1000 health queries
Extensive validation including 96-98% human-evaluator agreement, thorough ablation studies (Appendix F), and integrity checks for test case quality
Actionable findings: identifies that reasoning models and deeper scaffolds are significantly safer; shows common defenses (reminder prompting) are largely ineffective
Thoughtful handling of simulation-reality gap with detailed justification in Appendix J.3 for why simulation-based testing is necessary and preferable to real-world SEO manipulation
Excellent presentation with clear motivation, well-structured methodology, comprehensive appendices, and concrete examples of model behaviors
Responsible red-teaming with detailed Impact Statement addressing annotator safety, ethical LLM use, and reproducibility
Framework designed for extensibility and continuous supervision of search agent safety during development
weaknesses: Simulation-reality gap: websites injected in last position with single injection per query, which may not reflect how real SEO attacks rank or coordinate
Low retention rates for test case generation (6.8-6.9% for Harmful Output and Indirect Prompt Injection), raising questions about generation process quality and representativeness
Stealthiness not explicitly enforced in website generation; Figure 10 shows persuasiveness increases ASRs, suggesting generated websites may be easier to detect than real attacks
Limited scope: only evaluates Google Search (not Bing, DuckDuckGo, etc.); excludes proprietary deep research systems due to hooking requirement
Modest benchmark size (300 test cases) compared to some contemporary benchmarks; limited to English-language queries
Safety evaluator uses single judge (GPT-4.1-mini for all assessments), which could introduce systematic biases toward/against certain models
Limited exploration of defense mechanisms: only evaluates reminder prompting and filtering; doesn't propose or test novel mitigation strategies beyond evaluation
Incomplete statistical analysis: results averaged over 3 trials but no confidence intervals, significance tests, or sensitivity analysis for key findings
Knowledge-action gap identified (Section 4.3) but root causes underexplored and no solutions proposed beyond noting the phenomenon
Unclear generalization: findings specific to current models and architectures; applicability to future agents uncertain
